name: Whale shark
habitat: Tropical and warm-temperate open seas.
size: Around 9 m at maturity; adults can grow much larger.
description: Meet the biggest fish on Earth! Despite its name, a whale shark is a fish, not a whale. Its wide, flat head and enormous mouth help it collect a meal from the water around it. Instead of chasing one big dinner, it can take in water full of tiny animals and filter out the food.

Look closely at the pale spots and stripes across its back. That striking pattern is one of the best clues for recognising a whale shark. These ocean travellers live in warm seas and sometimes gather where there is lots of plankton to eat. A huge body can be powered by very small snacks!
facts: It is the largest living fish, but it still has gills like other sharks.
Plankton are tiny drifting organisms. Whale sharks eat these, along with fish eggs, small fish and other food.
Water flows back out through the gills while food is caught by filtering structures.
Its broad head has a mouth near the front, rather than tucked far underneath.
Although often seen near the surface, whale sharks also dive into much deeper water.
A whale shark has two dorsal fins on its back. The first is much bigger than the second.
Three raised ridges run along each side of its body. These are another clue to look for in a photograph.
Its underside is white, while the back can look grey, blue or brown beneath those pale markings.
The upper half of a young whale shark's tail is much longer than the lower half. An adult's tail looks more like a crescent.
It can draw food-rich water into its mouth by suction, instead of relying only on swimming forward with an open mouth.
There are 20 filtering pads inside its mouth: ten on each side. Think of them as part of a giant food-straining system.
Scientists have recorded whale sharks diving more than 1,900 metres below the surface.
They can return to familiar feeding sites, but also travel long distances between places where food is plentiful.
At Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia, seasonal gatherings are linked to rich supplies of tiny drifting animals.
Whale sharks give birth to live pups. Their young hatch from egg cases inside the mother rather than from eggs left on the seabed.

name: Epaulette shark
habitat: Shallow coral reefs around northern Australia and New Guinea.
size: Adults roughly 0.6–1 m; reported maximum about 1.07 m.
description: Some sharks cruise the open ocean. This little explorer takes a different route: it can wriggle and walk along the seabed using its paired fins! Its long, slender body and rounded fins help it move through shallow reef habitats, looking for a meal among sand and coral.

The name epaulette comes from the large dark spot above each pectoral fin, a little like a shoulder badge. Life on a reef flat can be tricky when the tide goes out and water holds less oxygen. Epaulette sharks have unusual adaptations for coping with those conditions, but they are still fish that belong in the sea.
facts: It bends its body and moves its pectoral and pelvic fins to walk over the bottom.
The shoulder spots have pale edges that help them stand out.
It hunts small animals such as crabs, shrimp and worms.
It is often most active around dawn and dusk.
Females lay egg cases. Tiny sharks hatch out rather than being born live.
Its broad, rounded paired fins work like little paddles. Special muscles and bones help it use those fins as feet.
It has two dorsal fins of similar size, set quite far back along its long body.
Small feelers called barbels sit near its nostrils, a useful feature to notice in a close-up photograph.
Young epaulette sharks have darker bands across their backs and tails. These change into a spotted pattern as the sharks grow.
It can push its snout into sand while searching for hidden food.
Both adults and young use suction to pull food into their mouths.
Adults tend to eat more crabs and shrimp, while younger sharks eat more worms and fish.
Reef pools can hold very little oxygen when the tide goes out. This species has unusual adaptations that help it cope for a time; that is not a reason to take one out of the water.
Egg cases are laid beneath coral heads. The museum describes them as roughly 9 centimetres long and 3.5 centimetres wide.
Newly hatched pups are only about 14 to 16 centimetres long. Even the biggest reported adults are only a little over a metre.

name: Blacktip reef shark
habitat: Shallow coral reefs and sand flats in the tropical Indo-Pacific.
size: Adults roughly 1–1.6 m; some reach about 1.8 m.
description: Those dark fin tips are a brilliant clue! A blacktip reef shark is a streamlined swimmer often found in shallow, clear water around tropical reefs. Its brownish upper body fades to a pale underside, while black markings make the fins easy to spot.

Rather than roaming across vast stretches of open ocean all the time, many blacktip reef sharks stay close to familiar reef areas. A reef offers food, shelter and different habitats close together, from sandy flats to coral edges. It is a busy neighbourhood for a curious shark.
facts: The black fin tips are often highlighted by paler markings next to them.
It is a different species from the blacktip shark, Carcharhinus limbatus. Similar names do not always mean the same shark!
It eats fish, crustaceans and cephalopods, the group that includes squid and octopuses.
Young are born live rather than hatching from egg cases on the seabed.
Researchers studying their movements have found that individuals can remain strongly attached to a local reef area.
Its snout is short and rounded, rather than long and pointed.
Its eyes have a horizontally oval outline, a detail you might spot in a close photograph.
The brownish back fades to a white underside. This light-and-dark arrangement is called countershading.
A pale band runs along its side, from near the anal fin towards the pectoral fins.
The skin is covered with tiny tooth-like scales called denticles, not the large overlapping scales of many familiar fish.
Its teeth have small serrations: tiny cutting edges rather like the teeth of a little saw.
It visits several connected coastal habitats, including sand flats, coral reefs and sometimes mangroves with the tide.
Across the tropical Indo-Pacific, it is found around many islands and coastlines, including the Maldives and northern Australia.
Most litters contain two to four pups, although reproduction varies between regions.
Newborns are about 33 to 59 centimetres long, and most adults stay below about 1.6 metres.

name: Whitetip reef shark
habitat: Coral reefs and reef caves in the Indo-Pacific and eastern tropical Pacific.
size: Adults usually about 1–1.8 m; rarely larger.
description: If you could peek into a quiet reef cave during the day, you might find a whitetip reef shark resting inside. Its slender body, rounded snout and bright white fin tips make it a very different neighbour from the blacktip reef shark.

When night arrives, this reef explorer becomes a hunter. It searches cracks and crevices for small animals that other sharks might struggle to reach. Unlike sharks that depend on swimming forward to move water over their gills, it can keep breathing while it rests. So a shark taking a break is not necessarily in trouble!
facts: The first dorsal fin and the upper tip of its tail have conspicuous white markings.
It often shelters near the bottom or in caves by day and feeds at night.
It can remain in a familiar reef area for months or even years.
Its slender shape helps it investigate narrow spaces in the reef.
It eats animals such as fish, crustaceans and molluscs.
It can keep water moving over its gills while resting. Not every shark has to swim constantly to breathe.
It has a broad, flattened head, a rounded snout and oval eyes.
Small dark spots dot the sides of its grey-brown body.
The second dorsal fin and the anal fin are nearly the same size, unlike the very unequal fins of some other sharks.
Resting places can be shared with other whitetip reef sharks. They do not always defend a cave as a private home.
Many live around reefs in water roughly 8 to 40 metres deep, although deeper sightings have been recorded.
Its range includes tropical islands such as Hawaii and the Galapagos, as well as many Indo-Pacific reefs.
It is not the silvertip shark. That larger species has different proportions and more extensive pale fin edges.
A tooth has a main point with smaller points beside it, rather than one simple smooth triangle.
Females give birth to small litters of live pups. Newborns are roughly 52 to 60 centimetres long.

name: Bonnethead
habitat: Warm, shallow coastal bays and estuaries of the western Atlantic.
size: Often about 1–1.2 m as an adult; maximum about 1.5 m.
description: Not every hammerhead has a head shaped like a wide hammer! The bonnethead has a smooth, rounded head that looks more like a small shovel. Its eyes sit at the ends of that broad head, giving this little shark a wonderfully distinctive outline.

Bonnetheads explore warm coastal shallows, bays and estuaries, often in groups. Their teeth are a useful toolkit: sharper teeth at the front help handle prey, while flatter teeth farther back crush harder food. For a crab-hunting shark, having the right tools makes a big difference.
facts: Its head has an evenly rounded front edge, a useful identification clue.
It is one of the smaller members of the hammerhead family.
Hard-shelled prey such as crabs are important in its diet.
Its rear teeth act like little crushing surfaces rather than all being sharp points.
Bonnetheads can gather in small schools, and females give birth to live pups.
The wide, flattened head of a hammerhead is called a cephalofoil. That is a wonderful word to practise saying!
Unlike several larger hammerheads, a bonnethead does not have a central notch cut into the front of its head.
Its eyes sit near the ends of the broad head, and the head rolls from side to side as it swims.
The first dorsal fin is tall, while the pectoral fins at its sides are relatively short.
Its colour can be grey or grey-brown, sometimes with a greenish tint, and its belly is white.
It follows warm water, moving towards warmer places in winter and returning to higher latitudes in summer.
It feeds during daylight hours, searching for crabs, shrimp, molluscs and small fish.
After crushing a meal with its back teeth, it uses suction to move the food towards its throat.
Females tend to be larger than males. Adults are often around 1 to 1.2 metres long.
Pups use shallow seagrass habitats during their early lives. These sheltered coastal areas are important nursery places.

name: Leopard shark
habitat: Sandy or muddy bays and estuaries of the eastern Pacific.
size: Adults average about 1.2–1.5 m; larger individuals occur.
description: With bold dark saddles across its back and blotches down its sides, the leopard shark is dressed for a very different habitat from a tropical coral reef. It often lives close to the bottom of sandy or muddy bays along the eastern Pacific coast.

Leopard sharks are strong swimmers and may form schools, sometimes alongside other kinds of sharks. They search for small fish and bottom-dwelling animals. Their patterned coats make them fun to recognise, but there is a naming twist: in some places people also call the unrelated zebra shark a leopard shark. The scientific name tells you exactly which species you have found.
facts: This leopard shark is Triakis semifasciata, not the zebra shark sometimes given the same common name.
Its range includes coastal waters from Oregon to the Gulf of California.
Its back markings include dark saddle shapes as well as smaller blotches.
It eats prey such as crabs, shrimp, worms and small fish.
It gives birth to live young, and newborn pups already have a shark shape.
It prefers temperate coastal water, which is generally cooler than the tropical sea around a coral reef.
It often swims close to sandy or muddy bottoms in bays and estuaries.
Large numbers live in San Francisco Bay and other big estuaries on the eastern Pacific coast.
Schools sometimes include other kinds of sharks, such as brown smooth-hounds, grey smooth-hounds and spiny dogfish.
Its back can look silver or bronze-grey, while its underside is much paler.
The tail is uneven: its upper lobe is longer and has a noticeable notch.
Its teeth form overlapping ridges, creating a broad, ridged surface across the jaws.
Newborn pups are about 20 to 23 centimetres long, much smaller than adults averaging roughly 1.2 to 1.5 metres.
A litter can contain several pups; the museum reports litters of four to 29.
The species name semifasciata means half-banded, referring to the striking markings on its body.

name: Coral Comet
habitat: The daydream reef
size: Three imaginary surfboards long
description: In our make-believe ocean, Coral Comet is the first friend to volunteer for a treasure hunt. Every turn leaves a trail of star-shaped bubbles, which is very useful for anyone who has forgotten the way home.

Its favourite treasure is a beautifully sorted pebble collection. Some are arranged in fives, some in tens, and one very special pebble is reserved for a friend who tried something difficult. This is a fantasy story, not a real shark species.
facts: Leaves a trail of tiny star-shaped bubbles.
Collects coral-colored pebbles in groups of five.
Keeps a pretend compass that points towards anyone who needs a friend.
Has a different treasure-hunt whistle for every day of the week.
Builds little pebble bridges for the lagoon's imaginary snails.
Packs five seaweed sandwiches for a make-believe expedition, then invites friends to share.
Its comet trail becomes a dotted treasure map when it swims in a circle.
Always puts borrowed treasures back before starting a new adventure.

name: Moonfin
habitat: The moonlit make-believe trench
size: One moonbeam long
description: When the pretend ocean grows quiet, Moonfin switches on its crescent-shaped glow and goes exploring. It likes counting the stars reflected on the surface, though a passing ripple can make it lose its place.
Moonfin keeps a notebook full of dream maps. Every map ends at a cosy nook with room for a friend and a bedtime story. Glowing moon fins and dream maps belong to our imagination, not shark science.
facts: A sleepy explorer with a glowing crescent fin.
Counts constellations before going to sleep.
Keeps its imaginary dream maps rolled inside an empty moon shell.
Turns down its pretend moonlight whenever a friend wants to rest.
Invents names for constellations, including the Great Wobbly Jellyfish.
Carries a tiny bedtime bell that only dream creatures can hear.
Arranges star pillows in equal rows for visiting explorers.
Writes tomorrow's adventure in a notebook that closes with a soft bubble-pop.

name: Bubble Buddy
habitat: Bubblegum lagoon
size: Six soap bubbles long
description: Bubble Buddy is the make-believe lagoon's most enthusiastic bubble artist. Rings, spirals and wobbly squares drift behind it like a floating gallery. Nobody has worked out how it makes the square ones.
Before a bubble show, it shares the tickets equally among its friends and leaves the front row for the smallest creatures. This bubble-making character is imaginary; it is not a real shark species.
facts: Blows bubble rings that never quite pop.
Keeps its treasures in perfectly equal groups.
Its imaginary square bubbles are reserved for very special birthdays.
Practises bubble spirals by counting turns in twos.
Runs a pretend bubble theatre with a front row for tiny creatures.
Makes a bubble umbrella for friends who dislike imaginary underwater rain.
Gives every visitor the same number of shiny pretend tickets.
Ends each show with one enormous bubble shaped like a smile.

name: Sunny Saw
habitat: The sunshine shallows
size: Two sunbeams long
description: Sunny Saw organises the best pretend picnics in the sunshine shallows. Its extraordinary nose is just the thing for dividing an imaginary birthday cake into fair shares, provided someone remembers the napkins.
When clouds roll over the make-believe sea, Sunny invites everyone to count rays of sunshine instead. This friendly character is a fantasy invention, not a description of a real sawshark.
facts: Its pretend saw-shaped nose cuts birthday cake, not fish.
Invites every sea creature to its counting picnics.
Keeps a pretend picnic list inside a bright yellow shell.
Makes sure the smallest guest gets a plate before anyone takes seconds.
Counts sunshine rays in tens when setting the imaginary table.
Its favourite make-believe cake is lemon-and-seafoam flavour.
Decorates party hats with patterns of yellow and blue shells.
Always leaves a little extra room for an unexpected friend.

name: Mint Mischief
habitat: The peppermint kelp forest
size: Four mint leaves long
description: Mint Mischief leaves little treasure clues between the leaves of an imaginary peppermint forest. Some clues are number patterns. Others are very bad drawings of where the treasure might be.
The game is never about tricking a friend into feeling stuck: another helpful clue is always waiting nearby. Peppermint kelp and this mischievous shark belong to our make-believe ocean.
facts: Hides tiny treasure maps in the kelp.
Always leaves a useful clue for a friend.
Its pretend peppermint forest smells like a freshly opened sweet tin.
Uses a different leaf shape for each step of a treasure trail.
Once drew the map upside down and discovered a brand-new imaginary cove.
Keeps spare hints in a pocket made from folded make-believe kelp.
Never hides another creature's belongings without asking first.
Ends every treasure game by sharing the prize equally.

name: Star Skipper
habitat: The starlight sea
size: Nine shooting stars long
description: Star Skipper spends imaginary evenings bouncing across a sea full of reflected stars. Its favourite challenge is making a new repeating pattern without using the same sparkle twice in a row.
When a pattern goes wrong, it calls the mistake a brand-new constellation and tries again. A star-skipping shark is a fantasy friend, not a species you could find on a real expedition.
facts: Skips across the waves like a pebble.
Loves making patterns with bright little stars.
Its imaginary landing spots glow softly for exactly one pretend wink.
Counts wave-hops in threes before trying a new pattern.
Calls a zigzag trail the Dancing Sea Cucumber constellation.
Keeps a scrapbook of surprising patterns made by happy mistakes.
Invites friends to finish a sparkle pattern rather than racing them.
Always checks that the pretend landing pool has room for everybody.

name: Peach Pirate
habitat: Peachy pirate cove
size: A treasure chest long
description: Peach Pirate has the least frightening pirate ship in the make-believe sea. Its flag is a fancy napkin, its treasure is mostly shiny buttons, and everyone is welcome aboard.

The captain's most important rule is that every crew member gets a fair share, including the tiny snail who polishes the anchor. This is an imaginary pirate adventure, not information about a real shark.
facts: Shares every imaginary treasure equally.
Its pirate flag is really a very fancy napkin.
The ship's pretend anchor is a spoon with a ribbon tied to it.
Keeps shiny buttons sorted into little groups inside a peach-coloured chest.
Says ahoy to the same imaginary snail every morning.
Uses a treasure map with a big friendly arrow instead of a scary skull.
Awards the crew extra napkins whenever a pretend picnic gets messy.
Its favourite pirate rule is that asking for help is a brave thing to do.

name: Cloud Cruiser
habitat: The upside-down sky ocean
size: One fluffy cloud long
description: Cloud Cruiser dreams of an upside-down ocean where clouds are soft islands and rain falls upwards. It carries a small pretend cushion for anyone who needs a rest between adventures.
Its maps change whenever the wind blows, so Cloud Cruiser has become very good at trying a different route. Sky oceans and cushion-carrying sharks are part of this fantasy story, not marine biology.
facts: Swims through clouds in its dreams.
Makes soft landing spots for tired explorers.
Its imaginary cloud islands drift into a new arrangement every afternoon.
Packs a pretend cushion instead of a heavy treasure chest.
Counts fluffy stepping-stones before choosing a route across the sky sea.
Keeps a rain-upwards umbrella for the silliest make-believe weather.
Draws dotted lines on maps to show places it has not explored yet.
Likes a quiet adventure just as much as a grand one.

name: Jelly Jester
habitat: The giggling grotto
size: Seven jellybeans long
description: Jelly Jester is the chief entertainer of an imaginary grotto, wearing a hat that looks suspiciously like a jellyfish. Its jokes are so silly that even the pretend seaweed seems to wiggle with laughter.
Before each show, it arranges seats into equal rows so nobody is left behind a rock. This jellybean-sized jester is invented, not a real shark with scientific facts.
facts: Wears a hat made from a pretend jellyfish.
Knows a different silly joke for every times table.
Its imaginary stage curtain is a very polite piece of seaweed.
Practises bowing without letting the pretend jellyfish hat slip off.
Arranges audience seats in equal rows with a clear path for little guests.
Keeps jokes on coloured cards so friends can choose their favourite.
A joke that makes nobody laugh becomes a riddle for the next show.
Always lets an audience member say pass instead of joining in.

name: Kelp Knight
habitat: The secret seaweed castle
size: Two seaweed swords long
description: Kelp Knight guards a pretend castle built from folded seaweed. There are no battles here: its brave deeds include helping a lost fish and asking for help with a tricky treasure map.
Its leafy shield doubles as a picnic tray, and its helmet has a special opening for bubbles. This gentle knight lives in our imagination, not in a real species guide.
facts: Protects the smallest fish with a leafy shield.
Practises brave deeds, never battles.
Its imaginary castle has a drawbridge wide enough for two friends.
Uses the shield as a picnic tray on peaceful pretend patrols.
Keeps spare seaweed helmets for visitors who want to dress up.
Counts castle windows in fours when checking the bedtime lights.
Its bravest badge celebrates the day it asked someone else for help.
Every creature is welcome through the make-believe castle gate.

name: Rainbow Ripple
habitat: The rainbow tide pool
size: A whole rainbow long
description: Rainbow Ripple paints our make-believe tide pool with waves of changing colour. It loves arranging shells into patterns, then inviting a friend to guess what comes next.
Sometimes the best pattern is a completely surprising one. Rainbow Ripple keeps a special corner for happy accidents. Colour-changing rainbow fins are fantasy, not a claim about real sharks.
facts: Its fins change color with every happy thought.
Makes ripples in repeating patterns.
Its imaginary paintbrush is a ribbon of rainbow seaweed.
Collects shells that almost match, because almost can look wonderful.
Leaves one space in each pretend pattern for a friend's idea.
Invented a new make-believe colour called giggle-green.
Keeps happy accidents in a special corner of the rainbow pool.
Enjoys quiet grey days too, when the pretend colours can take a rest.

name: Disco Dorsal
habitat: The underwater dance floor
size: Five dance steps long
description: Disco Dorsal runs an imaginary dance party where every fin is welcome. Its glitter-ball dorsal fin turns the cave ceiling into a field of little stars, even when its dance steps go in the wrong direction.
The music comes in groups of eight beats, but nobody has to keep up. Taking a break is part of a good party. This disco shark is a fantasy character, not a real glowing species.
facts: Has a glitter-ball fin and two left flippers.
Always dances in groups of eight beats.
Its imaginary dance floor has a cosy quiet corner with soft cushions.
Counts everyone in before starting a new pretend dance.
Invented the Wobbly Seaweed Shuffle after stepping the wrong way.
Keeps the make-believe music gentle enough for little ocean ears.
Invites sitting, swaying and watching as well as full-fin dancing.
Ends every party by thanking the friends who helped tidy up.

name: Great white shark
habitat: Coastal and offshore waters, especially temperate seas around the world.
size: Large adults can reach around 6 m; females usually grow larger than males.
description: A great white is not white all over! Its grey upper body meets a pale belly along a sharp boundary. From above, the dark back can blend into deeper water; from below, the pale underside blends with the brighter surface. Its pointed nose and strong crescent-shaped tail belong to a traveller built for swimming.

Scientists use tags to follow these sharks between coastal feeding areas and the open ocean. An individual may make a long journey and later return to a familiar place. Great whites are wild predators, not movie monsters: learning how they really live is much more interesting than a scary story.
facts: Its scientific name is Carcharodon carcharias; white shark is another common name.
The body narrows towards both the snout and the tail, making a streamlined shape.
The snout is conical, rather like a rounded cone.
Its first dorsal fin is large, while the second dorsal fin is tiny.
The anal fin on the underside is also very small.
The tail has a crescent-like outline that helps power swimming.
A firm ridge, called a keel, runs along each side of the tail base.
The large teeth are triangular with serrated edges.
The lower teeth are generally more slender than the upper teeth.
Tiny tooth-like skin scales are called dermal denticles.
Fish are important food, and larger individuals also eat marine mammals such as seals.
It can keep parts of its body warmer than the surrounding water.
Tagging studies show journeys between coastal habitats and offshore waters.
Young are born live rather than hatching from eggs left on the seabed.
Newborn pups are already roughly 1 to 1.6 metres long.

name: Tiger shark
habitat: Tropical and warm-temperate seas, from coastal shallows to offshore waters.
size: Large adults commonly around 3.3–4.3 m, with some growing larger.
description: Look for the stripes! Young tiger sharks have especially clear dark bars and spots along their sides. The markings become less obvious as the shark grows, so an older tiger shark may not look very stripy at all. Its broad, blunt head is another useful clue.

This ocean explorer eats many different kinds of food and visits many kinds of habitat. It may search near a reef, cross a sandy area or head into deeper water. Its changing pattern is a reminder that identifying an animal is easier when you use several clues, not just one colour.
facts: Its name comes from dark markings that can resemble a tiger's stripes.
Young tiger sharks have clearer stripes than most adults.
Its head is broad with a noticeably blunt snout.
The front of the body is thick and becomes slimmer towards the tail.
The first dorsal fin is much larger than the second.
A low ridge runs between the two dorsal fins.
The upper lobe of the tail is long and slender.
The belly is much paler than the back.
Its teeth have curved points and finely serrated edges.
A deep notch gives each tooth an unusual shape.
The upper and lower teeth are similar in shape.
Its varied food includes fish, squid, crustaceans and sea turtles.
It is a different species from the sand tiger shark despite their similar names.
Females give birth to live young rather than laying eggs on the seabed.
Newborn pups are roughly half to three-quarters of a metre long.

name: Bull shark
habitat: Warm coastal seas, estuaries and sometimes freshwater rivers.
size: Many adults are about 2–3 m long; some grow larger.
description: Most sharks stay in salty seawater, but a bull shark can travel into rivers too. Special body processes help it handle changing salt levels. An estuary, where river water meets the sea, can be an important part of this shark's world.

A bull shark has a sturdy body, a short rounded snout and relatively small eyes. Young sharks can use sheltered coastal places as nursery habitat before moving more widely. Its remarkable ability to enter fresh water does not mean every shark can do the same thing!
facts: Bull sharks can live in seawater and also enter fresh water.
They have been recorded far upstream in some large rivers.
Their bodies regulate salts as they move between different kinds of water.
The body is noticeably stocky rather than very slender.
The snout is short, broad and rounded.
Its eyes are small compared with those of many related sharks.
The first dorsal fin is large and broadly triangular.
The second dorsal fin is much smaller than the first.
The pectoral fins are broad and angular.
It has no raised ridge between the dorsal fins.
Young individuals can have darker fin tips that fade as they grow.
Its upper teeth are broad and triangular with serrated edges.
Bony fish make up an important part of its food.
Pups are born live after developing inside their mother.
Sheltered coastal lagoons and estuaries can act as nurseries for the young.

name: Great hammerhead
habitat: Warm coastal and offshore waters, including continental shelves and coral reefs.
size: Often around 3–4 m as a large adult; exceptional individuals can approach 6 m.
description: This hammerhead makes a dramatic silhouette! Its very tall first dorsal fin curves backwards, and an adult's wide head has an almost straight front edge. The head shape is called a cephalofoil. It is part of the shark's real body, not a tool it carries around.

Compare it with the scalloped and smooth hammerheads in your album. All have wide heads, but their outlines are different. A great hammerhead also has curved rear edges on its pelvic fins, giving careful shark detectives another clue to investigate.
facts: It is the largest species of hammerhead shark.
The scientific name is Sphyrna mokarran.
An adult's head has a nearly straight front margin.
A shallow notch sits in the centre of that front margin.
A young great hammerhead's head is more curved than an adult's.
The first dorsal fin is unusually tall.
That dorsal fin curves backwards like a sickle.
The second dorsal fin is also relatively high.
The pelvic fins have curved rear margins.
The rear edge of the anal fin has a deep notch.
Its diet includes stingrays, other fish and invertebrates.
It swims in tropical and warm-temperate seas.
It can visit both coastal habitats and offshore waters.
Females give birth to live pups.
Newborn pups are roughly 50 to 70 centimetres long.

name: Scalloped hammerhead
habitat: Tropical and warm-temperate coastal waters, continental shelves and offshore islands.
size: Adults commonly about 2.5–3.5 m; some grow over 4 m.
description: The front edge of this shark's wide head has a wavy, scalloped outline. A notch in the middle and smaller indentations to either side help give it its name. Its first dorsal fin rises above a slim body, while the second dorsal fin is much smaller.

Scalloped hammerheads are famous for forming groups, including gatherings around some offshore islands. Young sharks use coastal nursery habitats. Scientists study both the groups and the journeys between them to understand which places matter throughout the sharks' lives.
facts: The broad head has a curved front edge rather than a straight one.
A central indentation and smaller side notches create the scalloped outline.
Its mouth is broadly arched.
The first dorsal fin is much larger than the second.
Its pelvic fins have straighter rear edges than those of a great hammerhead.
The back is grey to brownish grey and the underside is lighter.
Scalloped hammerheads sometimes form large schools.
They can gather around oceanic islands and seamounts.
Young sharks spend early life in inshore nursery areas.
Their food includes small schooling fish.
Squid and octopuses are also on the menu.
They also eat rays and some other sharks.
Females give birth to live pups rather than laying seabed egg cases.
Newborn pups are only a fraction of an adult's length, roughly 31 to 57 centimetres.
The closely related Carolina hammerhead looks extremely similar; scientists may need genetic or internal anatomical evidence to tell them apart.

name: Smooth hammerhead
habitat: Temperate and warm seas, often near continental shelves.
size: Large adults can reach around 4 m.
description: The smooth hammerhead has a head-shaped clue right in its name. Unlike its scalloped cousin, it has no notch in the middle of its rounded front edge. Look carefully at the outline and imagine tracing it with a pencil: a smooth curve across the centre!

This species visits cooler waters than many other large hammerheads. It eats fish and squid and can travel in groups. Its olive-grey back and pale underside suit an ocean traveller, while its wide head makes it instantly recognisable as a member of the hammerhead family.
facts: The front of the head is broad, flattened and rounded.
There is no central notch in the head's front edge.
Small indentations still occur near the nostrils on either side.
Its mouth has a strongly curved outline.
The back can be olive or brownish grey.
The underside is white.
It has no ridge running between the two dorsal fins.
The first dorsal fin is moderately tall with a curved outline.
The second dorsal fin is much lower.
Its pelvic fins are not strongly sickle-shaped.
It occurs in temperate seas as well as warmer waters.
Fish and squid are major parts of its diet.
It also eats some crustaceans and rays.
Young are born live.
Newborn pups measure roughly 50 to 61 centimetres long.

name: Shortfin mako
habitat: Tropical and temperate open seas, sometimes approaching coastal waters.
size: Adults often about 2–3 m, with large individuals reaching around 4 m.
description: A pointed nose, sleek body and powerful crescent tail make the shortfin mako an impressive ocean swimmer. Its back can look metallic blue, with a bright white underside. It chases fast-moving fish, so a shape that moves efficiently through water is very useful.

There is also a longfin mako! As you might guess, that species has longer pectoral fins. The shortfin mako's pale mouth area is another identification clue. Scientists study these slow-growing sharks carefully because females take many years to reach breeding age.
facts: Its body is streamlined, thick in the middle and narrow towards the ends.
The snout is pointed.
The eyes are large and dark.
The upper body is often a metallic blue colour.
The underside and the area around the mouth are pale.
Its powerful tail is crescent-shaped.
A prominent keel runs along each side of the tail base.
The pectoral fins are shorter than those of the longfin mako.
There are two living mako species: shortfin and longfin.
It can travel across entire oceans.
It eats fast-swimming fish such as tuna and swordfish.
Squid also form part of its diet.
It sometimes leaps out of the water.
Females give birth to live pups.
Females take many years to mature, making rapid population recovery difficult.

name: Blue shark
habitat: Temperate and tropical open oceans around the world.
size: Adults commonly around 2–3 m; some grow larger.
description: Meet a shark with long, wing-like pectoral fins and a beautiful blue back. Its slender body and pointed snout are quite different from the sturdy shape of a bull shark. Beneath that blue upper surface, the belly is a sharply contrasting white.

Blue sharks are open-ocean travellers. They follow food and suitable water conditions across great stretches of sea, sometimes gathering where there are schools of fish. Their long fins and narrow bodies make a distinctive silhouette, even when colour is hard to see underwater.
facts: Its dark blue back gives the blue shark its common name.
The belly is a bright, contrasting white.
This dark-above, light-below pattern is called countershading.
The body is unusually slender for a large shark.
The snout is long and cone-shaped.
Its eyes are large.
The pectoral fins are very long and pointed.
Its first dorsal fin sits relatively far back on the body.
It inhabits open ocean rather than only coral reefs.
It can make long-distance journeys.
Small schooling fish such as sardines and herring are important food.
It also eats squid and other soft-bodied ocean animals.
Blue sharks often feed at night but can feed during the day too.
They sometimes gather around schools of prey.
Females give birth to live pups, usually measuring about 35 to 50 centimetres.

name: Basking shark
habitat: Temperate seas worldwide, including coastal waters rich in plankton.
size: Adults often around 6.7–8.8 m, with some growing larger.
description: That enormous open mouth is collecting a very small dinner! A basking shark swims through patches of plankton and strains food from the water. Its huge gill slits almost wrap around its head, giving this giant a very different look from a hunting shark.

Only the whale shark grows larger among living fishes. Despite its size, the basking shark relies on tiny drifting animals for food. Watching one filter-feed is a wonderful reminder that a big body does not always need big prey.
facts: It is the second-largest living fish, after the whale shark.
It filters small planktonic animals from seawater.
It often swims with its mouth wide open while feeding.
Forward swimming pushes water through the mouth and towards the gills.
Structures called gill rakers help strain food from the water.
The long gill slits nearly encircle the head.
Its eyes look small beside its enormous mouth.
The snout has a conical shape.
Its tail is crescent-shaped.
The back is usually greyish brown but can look much darker.
It has many tiny teeth despite not using them to catch large prey.
A large oil-rich liver helps the shark stay buoyant.
It visits places where plankton gathers near the surface.
It lives mainly in temperate waters rather than tropical coral lagoons.
Its breeding biology is still poorly understood; scientists have much more to discover.

name: Sand tiger shark
habitat: Coastal waters, sandy bays and rocky reefs in several warm and temperate regions.
size: Large adults are often around 2–3 m long.
description: Those slender teeth can stick out even when the mouth is closed, but teeth alone do not tell an animal's whole story. Sand tiger sharks often swim slowly around reefs and coastal habitats. Their grey-brown bodies may carry scattered reddish-brown spots.

This species has several common names: sand tiger shark, grey nurse shark and spotted ragged-tooth shark. It is not the same as the tiger shark or the nurse shark elsewhere in your album. Scientific names help people around the world make sure they mean the same animal.
facts: Its scientific name is Carcharias taurus.
In Australia it is commonly called the grey nurse shark.
Spotted ragged-tooth shark is another common name.
It is a separate species from the striped tiger shark.
The snout is pointed and somewhat flattened.
The long mouth extends behind the eyes.
Its teeth have slender central points with smaller side points.
The first dorsal fin sits relatively far back on the body.
The two dorsal fins are fairly similar in size.
The upper lobe of the tail is much longer than the lower lobe.
Dark reddish or brown spots can dot the sides.
It can gulp air at the surface and hold it in its stomach to help control buoyancy.
Its food includes bony fish, squid and crustaceans.
Sand tiger sharks sometimes gather in groups.
Females usually give birth to two large live pups.

name: Nurse shark
habitat: Warm Atlantic coastal habitats, including reefs, seagrass beds and sandy shallows.
size: Large adults are often around 2–3 m long.
description: A nurse shark can rest on the seabed while moving water over its gills. During the day, several may share a sheltered resting place. At night this bottom explorer becomes more active, looking for small animals tucked among the reef and sand.

Look for the rounded fins, long tail and small feelers near the mouth. Those feelers are called barbels. Its mouth may look small, but the shark can use powerful suction to draw food out of awkward hiding places. Resting sharks still need space and should never be touched.
facts: It can breathe while resting rather than swimming all the time.
It often rests by day and searches for food at night.
Several nurse sharks may gather at a resting site.
Adults can be light tan to dark brown.
Small juveniles have dark spots that are not obvious in adults.
There are two rounded dorsal fins without spines.
The first dorsal fin is larger than the second.
The first dorsal fin begins above the pelvic fins.
The tail makes up more than a quarter of its total length.
The small mouth is positioned well in front of the eyes.
Barbels hang near the nostrils and mouth.
It uses suction to help pull food into its mouth.
Its food includes fish, squid, octopuses and crustaceans.
Young are born live after developing inside the mother.
The tawny nurse shark is a separate Indo-Pacific species, not another colour of this shark.

name: Lemon shark
habitat: Warm coastal shallows, sandy or muddy bottoms, mangroves and estuaries.
size: Large adults commonly about 2.4–3 m long.
description: A lemon shark is not bright yellow like a lemon sweet. Its back is more yellow-brown or olive-grey, helping it blend into sandy coastal places. Two dorsal fins of similar size make a handy identification clue, because many sharks have a much smaller second fin.

Shallow nursery habitats are especially important to young lemon sharks. Females return to nursery areas to give birth, and the young may spend years there. Mangroves and protected coastal waters can therefore matter just as much to a shark as the open sea.
facts: Its yellowish-brown colour inspired the name lemon shark.
The underside is a paler yellowish white.
The body is stocky rather than very narrow.
The snout is short, blunt and rounded.
The two dorsal fins are similar in size and shape.
The first dorsal fin sits behind the pectoral fins.
There is no ridge running between the two dorsal fins.
Its body lacks bold stripes or spots.
It often swims over sand or mud.
Bony fish are a major part of its diet.
Crustaceans such as crabs are also on the menu.
Females give birth to live pups.
Mothers return to shallow nursery grounds to give birth.
Young sharks can stay in those nursery areas for several years.
Newborn pups measure roughly 50 to 60 centimetres long.

name: Sandbar shark
habitat: Coastal continental shelves, bays and estuaries in warm and temperate seas.
size: Adults often about 1.5–2 m long, with some larger individuals.
description: The sandbar shark has a fin that really stands out: a tall triangular first dorsal fin. Its body is deep and sturdy, its snout is rounded, and its plain grey-brown colour has none of a tiger shark's bold stripes. Try spotting the fin before looking at the name!

This shark searches near the seabed for small fish and other animals. Young sandbar sharks use sheltered bays and estuaries as nurseries. As with many coastal sharks, protecting shallow habitats helps protect an important stage of its life.
facts: Its very tall first dorsal fin is a useful identification feature.
The first dorsal fin starts above or a little ahead of the pectoral-fin base.
Its snout is blunt and rounded.
A low ridge runs between the dorsal fins.
The upper body is bluish grey to brownish grey.
The underside is paler and may look white.
It does not have conspicuous spots or body stripes.
Its upper teeth are broad and triangular.
The lower teeth are narrower than the upper teeth.
It searches near the bottom for food.
Small bony fish are important prey.
It also eats squid, octopuses and crustaceans.
It can feed during the day but becomes more active at night.
Young are born live.
Sheltered bays and estuaries provide nursery habitat.

name: Dusky shark
habitat: Warm and temperate continental coasts, from shallow waters to offshore shelf edges.
size: Large adults can grow to around 3–4 m.
description: A dusky shark can look like several of its grey coastal relatives, so a single colour is not enough for identification. Long swept-back pectoral fins, a relatively low rounded first dorsal fin and a small ridge along the back are useful pieces of the puzzle.

These sharks grow slowly and take a long time to reach adulthood. Females may move into coastal waters to give birth, while larger sharks range more widely. Their slow life cycle means that looking after adults and nursery habitats both matters.
facts: The back is generally bluish grey.
The underside is white.
Fin edges can look dusky, although the markings may be faint in adults.
The first dorsal fin is relatively low and rounded.
The pectoral fins are large and sickle-shaped.
A low ridge runs between the two dorsal fins.
The first dorsal begins near the free rear tips of the pectoral fins.
It can be confused with the similar Galapagos shark.
Dusky sharks are often associated with continental coastlines.
Bony fish form an important part of their diet.
They also eat cephalopods, the group containing squid and octopuses.
Crustaceans are another part of the menu.
The young are born live.
Females generally move inshore to give birth.
Pregnancy can last well over a year, and females do not breed every year.

name: Grey reef shark
habitat: Tropical Indo-Pacific coral reefs, especially reef slopes and drop-offs.
size: Adults often around 1.3–1.9 m long.
description: A broad dark border along the back edge of the tail is a useful clue for a grey reef shark. Its grey back fades to a pale belly, while the first dorsal fin is not boldly black-tipped like that of a blacktip reef shark. Similar reef neighbours can have very different details!

Grey reef sharks patrol reef edges and slopes, finding fish and other small ocean animals. They can gather near reefs, and much feeding activity happens at night. Giving wild sharks plenty of space lets them carry on with their own busy reef lives.
facts: It lives around coral reefs in the tropical Indo-Pacific.
Its back can be dark grey or bronze-grey.
The underside is white.
A broad dark margin runs along the rear edge of the tail.
The first dorsal fin is usually grey or irregularly edged with white.
Several other fins can have dark tips.
Its snout is broadly rounded.
The eyes are relatively large.
There is no ridge between the two dorsal fins.
The pectoral fins are narrow and curved.
Reef fish are its main food.
It also eats squid and octopuses.
Crustaceans such as shrimp and lobsters are sometimes eaten.
Much of its feeding happens at night.
Females give birth to small litters of live pups, usually one to six.

name: Blacktip shark
habitat: Tropical and warm-temperate coastal waters, bays and estuaries.
size: Adults often around 1.5 m, with larger individuals exceeding 2 m.
description: This is not the same species as the blacktip reef shark already in your album! The blacktip shark has a more pointed snout, and scientists use fin details and other features to tell related sharks apart. Similar common names can be tricky, which is why scientific names are so helpful.

Blacktip sharks often hunt small schooling fish in coastal waters. Females give birth in sheltered nursery areas, where the young spend their early years. The little sharks already have dark markings on several fins, although those markings can become less obvious with age.
facts: Its scientific name is Carcharhinus limbatus.
The blacktip reef shark is the different species Carcharhinus melanopterus.
The snout is moderately long and pointed.
Its body is stout rather than extremely slender.
The first dorsal fin is high with a narrow pointed tip.
The pectoral fins are fairly large and pointed.
There is no ridge between the two dorsal fins.
The back is dark grey to brown and the belly is white.
A pale band is visible along the flank.
Several fins have conspicuous black tips.
Those dark markings tend to fade with age.
The anal fin usually lacks a black tip, unlike that of a larger spinner shark.
Small schooling fish such as sardines and anchovies are important food.
Females give birth to live pups.
Inshore estuaries can serve as nurseries for young blacktip sharks.

name: Zebra shark
habitat: Shallow tropical Indo-Pacific reefs and sandy seabeds.
size: Adults can reach around 2.5 m, including the very long tail.
description: A baby zebra shark wears stripes, but an adult wears spots! Youngsters have pale bands against a dark body. As they grow, their pattern changes dramatically, leaving adults with dark spots on a yellowish-brown background. That is quite a wardrobe change.

The long tail and raised body ridges make an adult zebra shark distinctive. It often rests on the seabed by day and searches reef spaces for food at night. Some places call it a leopard shark, but it is not the Californian leopard shark, Triakis semifasciata, in this album.
facts: Its current scientific name is Stegostoma tigrinum.
Older sources and photo captions often use Stegostoma fasciatum.
Young zebra sharks have pale stripes and spots on a dark background.
Adults are yellow-brown with dark spots.
The juvenile stripes inspired the common name zebra shark.
Adults have five prominent ridges along the body.
The tail is almost as long as the main body.
The pectoral fins are broad and rounded.
Short barbels sit near the nostrils.
Breathing openings called spiracles lie behind the eyes.
It is often active at night.
It uses suction to take food from reef crevices.
Its diet includes molluscs, crustaceans and small fish.
Females lay large egg cases rather than giving birth to live pups.
Hair-like fibres on the egg cases help attach them to the seabed.

name: Tawny nurse shark
habitat: Tropical Indo-Pacific reefs, lagoons and sandy coastal bottoms.
size: Large individuals can grow to around 3 m or more.
description: This brown reef resident has a broad head and a small mouth that works like a powerful suction nozzle. It searches holes and crevices for hidden food. Its pointed fin tips help distinguish it from the more round-finned nurse shark of the Atlantic.

Tawny nurse sharks can rest on the bottom as well as swim around the reef. Their grey-brown colour may vary with their surroundings, and youngsters can carry small dark spots. Despite a similar common name, this is its own species with its own Indo-Pacific home.
facts: The scientific name is Nebrius ferrugineus.
It is a different species from Ginglymostoma cirratum, the nurse shark.
It inhabits the Indo-Pacific region.
Its body is large and bulky.
The snout has a somewhat squared outline.
The small mouth sits well in front of the eyes.
Its teeth have a small central point and a comb-like outline.
The pectoral fins have pointed tips and curved outlines.
The first dorsal fin is larger than the second.
Both dorsal fins sit towards the rear of the body.
There are no raised ridges along its body.
Youngsters can have small dark spots.
It explores reef holes while looking for food.
It uses strong suction to draw food into its mouth.
Its food includes small fish, cephalopods, crustaceans and sea urchins.

name: Spotted wobbegong
habitat: Australian coastal reefs, rocky ledges and nearby seabeds.
size: Many are around 1.5–1.8 m; some grow considerably larger.
description: Can you spot the shark hiding in plain sight? A spotted wobbegong has a broad flattened body, patterned skin and little flaps around its head. Together these features help it blend into a busy reef background. It belongs to the group often called carpet sharks.

By day, it may rest beside rocks or beneath a ledge. At night it searches for food, and it can also wait for prey to come close. Looking without touching is important: camouflage does not make a wild animal a safe stepping stone!
facts: Its scientific name is Orectolobus maculatus.
It has a flattened body suited to life near the bottom.
Skin flaps fringe the mouth and sides of the head.
Barbels occur near the nostrils.
The upper body can look yellowish or greenish brown.
Large dark saddle markings cross the back.
Many pale ring-shaped markings decorate the body.
Its pattern helps it blend into the seabed.
The pectoral and pelvic fins are broad.
Large spiracles sit behind the eyes.
The dorsal fins do not have spines.
It often rests during the day.
It is an active hunter at night.
Food includes fish, crabs, lobsters and octopuses.
Females give birth to live pups rather than leaving egg cases on the seabed.

name: Port Jackson shark
habitat: Temperate coastal waters of southern Australia, especially rocky reefs and sandy bottoms.
size: Usually under 1.5 m, with females generally larger than males.
description: This little shark looks as if it is wearing a dark harness! Bold bands cross its pale body, while ridges above the eyes give its blunt head a distinctive shape. It belongs to the bullhead sharks, a different group from the much larger bull shark.

Its mouth contains two useful kinds of teeth: smaller pointed teeth at the front and broad crushing teeth farther back. Those back teeth help deal with hard-shelled food. Its egg case is just as remarkable, with a spiral shape that looks a little like a corkscrew.
facts: Dark harness-like bands help identify this species.
A dark band crosses the face near the eyes.
The head is blunt rather than pointed.
Prominent ridges rise above the eyes.
A spine sits in front of each dorsal fin.
The mouth is relatively small.
Grooves link the nostril region with the mouth.
The front teeth are small and pointed.
The teeth farther back are broad and suited to crushing.
Sea urchins are an important food.
It also eats molluscs and crustaceans.
Youngsters eat more soft-bodied food than adults.
Females lay egg cases rather than giving birth to live pups.
Each egg case has a distinctive spiral flange.
A hatchling is only about 18 to 22 centimetres long.
